1: # Configure Targets {#configure-targets}
2: 
3: After creating an empty project, we will get the following basic configuration file.
4: 
5: ```lua [xmake.lua]
6: add_rules("mode.debug", "mode.release")
7: 
8: target("test")
9:     set_kind("binary")
10:     add_files("src/*.cpp")
11: ```
12: 
13: Among them, `mode.release` is the default compilation mode rule, which will automatically add some common optimization compilation options for the target build, such as: `-O2`, and so on.
14: 
15: We can also switch to `mode.debug` debugging mode through `xmake f -m debug`, which will automatically configure some debugging options, such as: `-g`, and so on.
16: 
17: Of course, we can also configure them completely by ourselves without using the mode rules.
18: 
19: ```lua [xmake.lua]
20: target("test")
21:     set_kind("binary")
22:     add_files("src/*.cpp")
23: ```
24: 
25: For the complete `target()` API reference, see [Project Target Description API](/api/description/project-target). To access target instances in the script domain, see [Target Instance API](/api/scripts/target-instance).
26: 
27: ## Configure macro definition {#configure-defines}
28: 
29: We can add a macro definition option to the target program through [add_defines](/api/description/project-target#add-defines), for example:
30: 
31: ```lua [xmake.lua]
32: target("test")
33:     set_kind("binary")
34:     add_files("src/*.cpp")
35:     add_defines("DEBUG")
36: ```
37: 
38: In the test target scope, we configure a macro definition compilation option `-DDEBUG` for it, which will only take effect on the test target.
39: 
40: We can also use the `xmake -v` command to quickly verify whether the added configuration is effective.
41: 
42: ```sh
43: [ 23%]: cache compiling.release src/main.cpp
44: /Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer/Toolchains/XcodeDefault.xctoolchain/usr/bin/clang -c -Q
45: unused-arguments -target x86_64-apple-macos15.2 -isysroot /Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer/Platforms/MacOSX.platform/Developer/SDKs/MacOSX15.2.sdk -fvisibility=hidden -fvisibility-inline
46: s-hidden -O3 -DNDEBUG -o build/.objs/test/macosx/x86_64/release/src/main.cpp.o src/main.cpp
47: ```
48: 
49: As you can see, `-DDEBUG` has been added to the clang compilation command.
50: 
51: ## Configure multiple targets at the same time {#configure-multi-targets}
52: 
53: If you want multiple compilation targets to take effect at the same time, we can move them to the global root scope.
54: 
55: ```lua [xmake.lua]
56: add_defines("DEBUG")
57: 
58: target("foo")
59:     set_kind("binary")
60:     add_files("src/*.cpp")
61: 
62: target("bar")
63:     set_kind("binary")
64:     add_files("src/*.cpp")
65: ```
66: 
67: At this time, both foo and bar target programs will have the `-DDEBUG` compilation option.
68: 
69: The configuration of the root scope will affect the current xmake.lua configuration file and the target programs in all sub-xmake.lua files (that is, the sub-directory configuration introduced by includes).
70: 
71: ```lua [xmake.lua]
72: add_defines("DEBUG")
73: 
74: target("foo")
75:     set_kind("binary")
76:     add_files("src/*.cpp")
77: 
78: includes("bar")
79: ```
80: 
81: ```lua [bar/xmake.lua]
82: target("bar")
83:     set_kind("binary")
84:     add_files("src/*.cpp")
85: ```
86: 
87: If the bar target is in the `bar/xmake.lua` sub-configuration file, it will also be effective.
88: 
89: ::: tip NOTE
90: However, the root scope configuration in the sub-file cannot affect the target in the same level or parent configuration file.
91: :::
92: 
93: ```lua [xmake.lua]
94: target("foo")
95:     set_kind("binary")
96:     add_files("src/*.cpp")
97: 
98: includes("bar")
99: ```
100: 
101: ```lua [bar/xmake.lua]
102: add_defines("DEBUG")
103: 
104: target("bar")
105:     set_kind("binary")
106:     add_files("src/*.cpp")
107: 
108: target("zoo")
109:     set_kind("binary")
110:     add_files("src/*.cpp")
111: ```
112: 
113: Here, although `add_defines` is configured in the root scope, it only affects the bar and zoo targets, and cannot affect the foo target.
114: 
115: In other words, the scope of influence of the root scope is in a tree structure, and it takes effect layer by layer.
116: 
117: ## Configure optimization options {#configure-optimization}
118: 
119: `mode.release` will automatically introduce some optimization options, and we can also configure them ourselves through the [set_optimize](/api/description/project-target#set-optimize) interface.
120: 
121: For example:
122: 
123: ```lua
124: set_optimize("faster")
125: ```
126: 
127: It will configure the `-O2` compilation option for the target.
128: 
129: ::: tip NOTE
130: Different compilers have different optimization options, and xmake will automatically map to the most appropriate compilation option.
131: 
132: :::
133: 
134: For more details, please refer to the document: [set_optimize](/api/description/project-target#set-optimize).
135: 
136: ## Configure header file search directory {#configure-includedirs}
137: 
138: ```lua
139: add_includedirs("/tmp")
140: ```
141: 
142: It will add the `-I/tmp` compilation option to the compiler's command line.
143: 
144: For more details, please refer to the document: [add_includedirs](/api/description/project-target#add-includedirs).
145: 
146: ## Configure link library search directory {#configure-linkdirs}
147: 
148: ```lua
149: add_linkdirs("/tmp")
150: ```
151: 
152: It will add the `-L/tmp` link option to the linker command line.
153: 
154: For more details, please refer to the document: [add_linkdirs](/api/description/project-target#add-linkdirs).
155: 
156: ## Configure link library {#configure-links}
157: 
158: ```lua
159: add_links("foo")
160: ```
161: 
162: It will add the `-lfoo` link option to the linker command line, which usually needs to be used with [add_linkdirs](/api/description/project-target#add-linkdirs).
163: 
164: ```lua
165: add_links("foo")
166: add_linkdirs("/tmp")
167: ```
168: 
169: For more details, please refer to the document: [add_links](/api/description/project-target#add-links).
170: 
171: ## Configure system link library {#configure-syslinks}
172: 
173: `add_links` is usually used to link user-generated libraries, while `add_syslinks` can add system libraries without the need for an additional `add_linkdirs`.
174: 
175: And its link order is relatively late (after user libraries).
176: 
177: ```lua
178: add_links("foo")
179: add_syslinks("pthread", "dl")
180: ```
181: 
182: If links and syslinks are configured at the same time, the link order is as follows:
183: 
184: ```sh
185: -lfoo -lpthread -ldl
186: ```
187: 
188: ## Configure original compilation options {#configure-flags}
189: 
190: The `add_defines` and other interfaces mentioned above are all abstract APIs. Since most compilers support them, Xmake abstracts them to make them more convenient for users to use and provide better cross-platform and cross-compiler support.
191: 
192: However, we can also add specific compilation options for C++ code through the `add_cxxflags` interface, such as:
193: 
194: ```lua
195: add_cxflags("-DDEBUG")
196: ```
197: 
198: It is equivalent to `add_defines("DEBUG")`, but `add_defines` is more general and applicable to all compilers, while `add_cxxflags("-DDEBUG")` may only be applicable to a few compilers, because not all compilers define macros through `-D`.
199: 
200: In addition, we can also add compilation options for C code through the `add_cflags` interface, and `add_cxflags` to add compilation options for C/C++ code at the same time.
201: 
202: For more details, please refer to the documentation:
203: 
204: - [add_cflags](/api/description/project-target#add-cflags)
205: - [add_cxflags](/api/description/project-target#add-cxflags)
206: - [add_cxxflags](/api/description/project-target#add-cxxflags)
207: 
208: ## Target Type Configuration {#configure-target-types}
209: 
210: ### Setting Target Types
211: 
212: You can set different target types through `set_kind()`:
213: 
214: ```lua
215: target("app")
216:     set_kind("binary")      -- executable program
217:     add_files("src/*.cpp")
218: 
219: target("lib")
220:     set_kind("static")      -- static library
221:     add_files("src/*.cpp")
222: 
223: target("dll")
224:     set_kind("shared")      -- dynamic library
225:     add_files("src/*.cpp")
226: 
227: target("obj")
228:     set_kind("object")      -- object file collection
229:     add_files("src/*.cpp")
230: 
231: target("header")
232:     set_kind("headeronly")  -- header-only library
233:     add_headerfiles("include/*.h")
234: ```
235: 
236: ### Target Type Description
237: 
238: | Type | Description | Output Files |
239: |------|-------------|--------------|
240: | binary | Executable program | app.exe, app |
241: | static | Static library | libapp.a, app.lib |
242: | shared | Dynamic library | libapp.so, app.dll |
243: | object | Object file collection | *.o, *.obj |
244: | headeronly | Header-only library | No compilation output |
245: | phony | Virtual target | No output, only for dependency management |
246: 
247: ### Virtual Targets (phony)
248: 
249: Virtual targets don't generate actual files, they're only used for managing dependencies:
250: 
251: ```lua
252: target("test1")
253:     set_kind("binary")
254:     add_files("src/test1.cpp")
255: 
256: target("test2")
257:     set_kind("binary")
258:     add_files("src/test2.cpp")
259: 
260: target("all-tests")

1: # Syntax description
2: 
3: Xmake's project description file `xmake.lua` is based on the Lua syntax, but in order to make the project build logic more convenient and concise, Xmake encapsulates it, making writing `xmake.lua` not as cumbersome as some makefiles.
4: 
5: Basically, to write a simple project build description, just three lines, for example:
6: 
7: ```lua
8: target("test")
9:     set_kind("binary")
10:     add_files("src/*.c")
11: ```
12: 
13: For a complete list of available interfaces in the description and script domains, see [Description Domain API](/api/description/specification) and [Script Domain Built-in Modules](/api/scripts/builtin-modules/os).
14: 
15: ## Configuration Separation
16: 
17: Xmake.lua uses the 80:20 rule (aka [Pareto principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pareto_principle)) to implement a two-layer separate configuration of the description domain and the script domain.
18: 
19: What is the 80:20 rule? In short, most of the project configuration, 80% of the cases, are basic configurations, such as: `add_cxflags`, `add_links`, etc.
20: Only less than 20% of the space needs to be extra complex to meet some special configuration needs.
21: 
22: The remaining 20% of the configuration is usually more complicated. If it is directly flooded in the whole `xmake.lua`, the whole project configuration will be very confusing and very unreadable.
23: 
24: Therefore, Xmake isolates 80% of simple configuration and 20% of complex configuration by describing two different configurations: description domain and script domain, making the whole `xmake.lua` look very clear and intuitive, readable and maintainable. Get the best results.
25: 
26: ### Description Scope
27: 
28: For beginners who are just getting started, or just want to maintain some simple small projects, the requirements are fully met by describing the configuration completely. What is the description domain? It looks like this:
29: 
30: ```lua
31: target("test")
32:     set_kind("binary")
33:     add_files("src/*.c")
34:     add_defines("DEBUG")
35:     add_syslinks("pthread")
36: ```
37: 
38: At first glance, it is actually a configuration set of `set_xxx`/`add_xxx`. For the novice, you can use it not as a Lua script, but just as an ordinary, but there are some basic rules configuration file.
39: 
40: If, by looking, there are parentheses, or function calls like scripting languages, then we can also write this (whether with parentheses is up to personal preference):
41: 
42: ```lua
43: target "test"
44:     set_kind "binary"
45:     add_files "src/*.c"
46:     add_defines "DEBUG"
47:     add_syslinks "pthread"
48: ```
49: 
50: Is this looking more like a profile? In fact, the description field is a configuration file, similar to the configuration of keys/values such as JSON, so even if you are not familiar with Lua, you can quickly get started.
51: 
52: Moreover, for most projects, only the various settings of the project are configured by `set_xxx/add_xxx`, which has fully met the requirements.
53: 
54: This is what I said at the beginning: 80% of the time, you can use the simplest configuration rules to simplify the configuration of the project, improve readability and maintainability, so that users and developers will be very friendly and more intuitive.
55: 
56: What if we want to make some conditional judgments for different platforms and architectures? It doesn't matter, the description field, in addition to the basic configuration, also supports conditional judgment, as well as the for loop:
57: 
58: ```lua
59: target("test")
60:     set_kind("binary")
61:     add_files("src/*.c")
62:     add_defines("DEBUG")
63:     if is_plat("linux", "macosx") then
64:         add_links("pthread", "m", "dl")
65:     end
66: ```
67: 
68: ```lua
69: target("test")
70:     set_kind("binary")
71:     add_files("src/*.c")
72:     add_defines("DEBUG")
73:     for _, name in ipairs({"pthread", "m", "dl"}) do
74:         add_links(name)
75:     end
76: ```
77: 
78: Is this looking a bit like Lua? Although, it can usually be regarded as a common configuration problem, but Xmake is based on Lua after all, so the description domain still supports the basic language features of Lua.
79: 
80: However, it should be noted that although the description field supports Lua script syntax, try not to write too complicated Lua scripts in the description field, such as some time-consuming function calls and for loops.
81: 
82: And in the description field, the main purpose is to set the configuration item, so Xmake does not completely open all module interfaces. Many interfaces are forbidden to be called in the description field.
83: Even open callable interfaces are completely read-only, and time-consuming security interfaces such as `os.getenv()` read some general system information for configuration logic control.
84: 
85: Also note that `xmake.lua` is parsed multiple times to resolve different configuration fields at different stages: for example: `option()`, `target()`, etc.
86: 
87: So, don't think about writing complex Lua scripts in the description field of `xmake.lua`, and don't call print in the description field to display the information, because it will be executed multiple times, remember: it will be executed multiple times! ! !
88: 
89: ### Script Scope
90: 
91: Restrict the description field to write complex Lua, all kinds of Lua modules and interfaces are not used? How to do? This time is the time for the script domain to appear. If the user is already fully familiar with Xmake's description domain configuration and feels that some of the special configuration maintenance on the project is not met, then we can do more complex configuration logic in the script domain:
92: 
93: ```lua
94: target("test")
95:     set_kind("binary")
96:     add_files("src/*.c")
97:     on_load(function (target)
98:         if is_plat("linux", "macosx") then
99:             target:add("links", "pthread", "m", "dl")
100:         end
101:     end)
102:     after_build(function (target)
103:         import("core.project.config")
104:         local targetfile = target:targetfile()
105:         os.cp(targetfile, path.join(config.buildir(), path.filename(targetfile)))
106:         print("build %s", targetfile)
107:     end)
108: ```
109: 
110: As long as it is similar: `on_xxx`, `after_xxx`, `before_xxx`, etc. The script inside the function body belongs to the script field.
111: 
112: In the script domain, the user can do anything. Xmake provides an import interface to import various Lua modules built into Xmake, and can also import user-supplied Lua scripts.
113: 
114: We can implement any function you want to implement in the script domain, even if you write a separate project.
115: 
116: For some script fragments, if it is not very bloated, such as the above built-in writing is enough, if you need to implement more complex scripts, and do not want to be filled in a `xmake.lua`, you can separate the script into a separate Lua file for maintenance.
117: 
118: E.g:
119: 
120: ```lua
121: target("test")
122:     set_kind("binary")
123:     add_files("src/*.c")

13: -- affects both test and test2 targets
14: add_defines("DEBUG")

27: ## Visibility Settings {#visibility}
28: 
29: In xmake, many interfaces support `visibility` configuration parameters to control the visibility scope of configurations. The `visibility` parameter accepts an object containing the following key-value pairs:
30: 
31: | Key | Description | Example |
32: |-----|-------------|---------|
33: | `public` | Export to dependent sub-targets, when other targets depend on this target, they will inherit these configurations | `{public = true}` |
34: | `interface` | Export as interface, only effective for other targets that depend on this target, not effective for the current target itself | `{interface = true}` |
35: | `private` | Only effective for the current target, will not be passed to other targets that depend on this target | `{private = true}` |
36: 
37: ### Usage Examples
38: 
39: ```lua
40: -- Set public visibility, will be passed to other targets that depend on this target
41: add_defines("PUBLIC_DEFINE", {public = true})
42: 
43: -- Set interface visibility, only effective for other targets that depend on this target
44: add_includedirs("include", {interface = true})
45: 
46: -- Set private visibility, only effective for the current target
47: add_defines("PRIVATE_DEFINE", {private = true})
48: ```
49: 
50: ### Default Behavior
51: 
52: If the `visibility` parameter is not specified, most interfaces use `private` visibility by default, meaning configurations are only effective for the current target.

54: ## target

56: ### Define a project target
57: 
58: #### Function Prototype
59: 
60: ::: tip API
61: ```lua

63:     kind = <string>,
64:     files = <string|array>,
65:     ...
66: })
67: ```
68: :::
69: 
70: 
71: #### Parameter Description
72: 
73: | Parameter | Description |
74: |-----------|-------------|
75: | name | Target name string, used to identify the project target |
76: | kind | Target type string, optional values: binary, static, shared, object, headeronly, phony |
77: | files | Source file path string or array, supports wildcard matching patterns |
78: | ... | Other configuration options, such as deps, defines, includedirs, etc. |
79: 
80: #### Usage
81: 
82: Defines a console target named `test` in project and the default target filename is `test`.
83: 
84: ```lua

86:     set_kind("binary")
87:     add_files("src/*.c")
88: ```

6259: #### Matching output results
6260: 
6261: By default, `xmake test` will determine whether the test passed based on whether the exit code of the test run is 0.
6262: 
6263: Of course, we can also determine whether the test passes by configuring whether the output result of the test run meets our specified matching pattern.
6264: 
6265: Mainly controlled by these two parameters:
6266: 
6267: | Parameters | Description |
6268: | --- | --- |
6269: | pass_outputs | The test passes if the outputs match |
6270: | fail_outputs | If the outputs match, the test fails |
6271: 
6272: What is passed into `pass_outputs` and `fail_outputs` is a list of lua matching patterns, but the patterns are slightly simplified, such as the processing of `*`.
6273: 
6274: If the match is successful, the test passes and can be configured like this:
6275: 
6276: ```lua
6277: target("test")
6278:      add_tests("testname1", {pass_outputs = "hello"})
6279:      add_tests("testname2", {pass_outputs = "hello *"})
6280:      add_tests("testname3", {pass_outputs = {"hello", "hello *"}})
6281: ```
6282: 
6283: If the match is successful, the test fails. You can configure it like this:
6284: 
6285: ```lua
6286: target("test")
6287:      add_tests("testname1", {fail_outputs = "hello"})
6288:      add_tests("testname2", {fail_outputs = "hello *"})
6289:      add_tests("testname3", {fail_outputs = {"hello", "hello *"}})
6290: ```
6291: 
6292: We can also configure them simultaneously:
6293: 
6294: ```lua
6295: target("test")
6296:      add_tests("testname", {pass_outputs = "foo", fail_outputs = "hello"})
6297: ```
6298: 
6299: Since some test output results will have some newline or other blank characters at the end, which interferes with the matching mode, we can configure `trim_output = true` to truncate the blank characters before matching.
6300: 
6301: ```lua
6302: target("test")
6303:      add_tests("testname", {trim_output = true, pass_outputs = "foo", fail_outputs = "hello"})
6304: ```
6305: 
6306: We can also configure `{plain = true}` to disable lua pattern matching and only do the most basic flat text matching.
6307: 
6308: ```lua
6309: target("test")
6310:      add_tests("testname", {plain = true, pass_outputs = "foo", fail_outputs = "hello"})
6311: ```
6312: 
6313: We can also match the file content through `pass_output_files` and `fail_output_files`. The path inside is relative to the current `xmake.lua` script directory.
6314: 
6315: The content of the file specified by `pass_output_files` will serve as the expected standard output. If the actual output matches the file content, the test passes.
6316: 
6317: ```lua
6318: target("test")
6319:     set_kind("binary")
6320:     add_files("src/*.cpp")
6321:     add_tests("test1", {
6322:         runargs = {"arg1"},
6323:         pass_output_files = "test1.out"
6324:     })
6325: ```
6326: 
6327: #### Configure test group
6328: 
6329: We can also configure a test group through `group = "foo"` for group testing:
6330: 
6331: ```lua

3163: ## add_includedirs
3164: 
3165: ### Add include search directories
3166: 
3167: #### Function Prototype
3168: 
3169: ::: tip API
3170: ```lua
3171: add_includedirs(includedirs: <string|array>, ..., {
3172:     public|interface|private = <boolean>
3173: })
3174: ```
3175: :::
3176: 
3177: 
3178: #### Parameter Description
3179: 
3180: | Parameter | Description |
3181: |-----------|-------------|
3182: | includedirs | Header file search directory string or array, supports wildcard matching patterns |
3183: | ... | Variable parameters, can pass multiple header file search directory strings |
3184: | public\|interface\|private | Visibility setting, see [Visibility Settings](#visibility) for details |
3185: 
3186: #### Usage
3187: 
3188: Set the search directory for the header file. This interface is used as follows:
3189: 
3190: ```lua
3191: target("test")
3192:     add_includedirs("$(builddir)/include")
3193: ```
3194: 
3195: Of course, it can also be set directly through interfaces such as [add_cxflags](#add_cxflags) or [add_mxflags](#add_mxflags), which is also possible.
3196: 
3197: After 2.2.5, includedirs can be exported to dependent child targets via the extra `{public|interface = true}` property setting, for example:
3198: 
3199: ```lua
3200: target("test")
3201:     set_kind("static")
3202:     add_includedirs("src/include") -- only for the current target
3203:     add_includedirs("$(builddir)/include", {public = true}), the current target and child targets will be set
3204: 
3205: target("demo")
3206:     set_kind("binary")
3207:     add_deps("test")
3208: ```
3209: 
3210: For more on this block, see: [add_deps](#add_deps)
3211: 
3212: ::: tip NOTE
3213: If you don't want it to be fixed in the project, you can set it by: xmake f --includedirs=xxx or xmake f --cxflags="-I/xxx". This manual setting has higher directory search priority.
3214: :::
3215: 
3216: :::tip NOTE
3217: The header file does not support pattern matching by default, and it is not recommended to do so. It is easy to introduce some unnecessary subdirectories, resulting in the interference of various header file reference conflicts, and it is more difficult to check if there is a problem.
3218: :::
3219: If the user insists on doing this, it can be achieved by `add_includedirs(os.dirs(path.join(os.scriptdir(), "xxx/**")))`.
